speaker: John Carmack
title: John Carmack: Doom, Quake, VR, AGI, Programming, Video Games, and Rockets (#309)
question: In long-lived software systems, what hidden operational risk do unbounded dynamic collections introduce compared to fixed capacity limits paired with assertions?
guest: Assertions are active comments. In theory, if everything operates the way you expected, they will never fire. But even if you wrote the code completely right initially, circumstances change—the world outside your program changes. That's why I'm fond in many cases of static array size declarations. I went through a period where, because we had general collection classes, it seemed like a good idea to make everything completely variable and generic so it could grow up to whatever. There are cases where that's right, but it's also good to be informed when the world has changed more than you thought it would. If you have a continuously growing collection, you're never going to find out. You might have a quadratic slowdown on something where you thought you'd only ever have a handful of items, and then a new design style arrives and suddenly you have 10,000 of them. So I like picking a nice round power-of-two limit and adding an assert saying, 'Hey, you hit this limit—you should think about whether your choices are still relevant if someone is using ten times more than you expected.'

points.core: External usage patterns inevitably shift beyond the assumptions originally baked into working code.
points.note: Accept: even initially correct software faces changing workloads, design styles, or 10x–100x growth in item counts over its lifespan. Do not credit: generic statements that requirements change over time without tying to scale assumptions.

points.core: Unbounded collections silently absorb massive growth without warning engineers that core assumptions broke.
points.note: Accept: dynamically resizing arrays or generic containers mask order-of-magnitude workload increases because they never trigger a visible failure when limits are exceeded. Do not credit: generic memory-leak or OOM warnings without mentioning masked assumption shifts.

points.core: Silent collection growth triggers hidden algorithmic degradation such as quadratic slowdowns in production.
points.note: Accept: algorithms chosen for a handful of elements suffering O(n^2) or severe performance collapse once item counts unexpectedly reach thousands. Do not credit: vague claims that dynamic allocation is slower than static arrays.

points.core: Fixed limits with assertions act as alarms forcing engineers to re-evaluate scaled architectures.
points.note: Accept: explicit caps (e.g., power-of-two array sizes) paired with assertions alert developers when usage exceeds expectations so they can revisit data structures or algorithms. Do not credit: claiming fixed limits are always better than dynamic collections in every case.

models.label: Claude Fable 5.2
models.answer:
Unbounded dynamic collections hide the risk of silent, gradual resource exhaustion. Because a growable list, map, queue, or cache never refuses an insert, a leak, a missed eviction, a slow consumer, or an unexpected input pattern does not fail at the point of the mistake. Instead, memory creeps upward over days or months, and the symptoms appear far from the cause: rising garbage-collection pauses or allocator fragmentation, latency spikes when a large buffer reallocates and copies, degraded cache behaviour, and eventually an out-of-memory kill at an unpredictable moment, often under peak load and with no clear pointer to the offending structure. Short tests rarely reveal this, since the growth only matters at production uptimes.

A fixed capacity with an assertion turns that implicit assumption ("this never holds more than N items") into an explicit, checked invariant. Violations fail immediately, loudly, and at the exact site, which makes them easy to diagnose. Worst-case memory and latency become statically knowable, and the designer is forced to decide up front what happens on overflow, such as backpressure, shedding, or rejection.

models.label: Gemini Carbon
models.answer:
Unbounded dynamic collections mask missing backpressure, stalled consumers, and subtle retention bugs by allowing memory to grow silently until the system suffers catastrophic, non-local failure. Because physical memory is always finite, an unbounded structure does not remove limits; it merely defers enforcement to the allocator or operating system. In long-lived systems, this deferral introduces progressive heap fragmentation, unpredictable reallocation stalls, garbage-collection thrashing, and severe tail-latency degradation long before an out-of-memory killer terminates the process—often crashing an unrelated operation far in time and call stack from the root cause. Worse, unbounded growth hides defects during testing because short runs and modest workloads succeed effortlessly, turning logic errors or unhandled traffic spikes into delayed, non-deterministic outages weeks into production.

By contrast, fixed capacity limits paired with assertions turn implicit resource exhaustion into an explicit invariant. They compel upfront backpressure and eviction design, guarantee predictable memory footprints, and fail fast at the exact point where an assumption is violated, surfacing bugs deterministically during testing rather than letting them lurk as operational time bombs.

models.label: Claude Opus 5.5
models.answer:
The hidden risk is slow, silent growth that fails late and far from its cause. An unbounded list, map, or queue works fine in testing and early production. Then, after weeks of uptime, a traffic spike, a slow consumer, or a small leak lets it grow without limit. Nothing flags the problem. Instead, memory pressure builds, garbage-collection pauses and latency get worse, the heap fragments, and the process eventually gets killed for running out of memory, often at an awkward moment and with no clear link to the code that caused it. Because the worst case was never defined, nobody tested it, so the system's real capacity is unknown.

A fixed capacity limit checked by an assertion changes that. Exceeding the limit fails right away, loudly, and at the exact spot where an assumption broke. The worst-case memory and latency can be calculated and tested. Designers also have to decide up front what happens at the limit: apply backpressure, shed load, or reject the request. This is why NASA's "Power of Ten" rules and TigerBeetle's TigerStyle say to put an explicit limit on everything. It turns gradual, hard-to-diagnose decay into a predictable failure you can find and fix.

models.label: Gemini Neon
models.answer:
Unbounded dynamic collections introduce the hidden risk of silent, delayed resource exhaustion that masks underlying design or operational flaws until the system fails catastrophically. Because these structures quietly grow to absorb unexpected traffic spikes, stalled consumers, retry storms, or forgotten evictions, they allow pathological state to accumulate invisibly over hours or weeks. Instead of failing immediately when an assumption breaks, the process gradually degrades through worsening garbage-collection pauses, cache thrashing, and tail-latency spikes before abruptly dying from an out-of-memory kill—often far removed in time and stack trace from the actual root cause.

By contrast, fixed capacity limits paired with assertions force engineers to define explicit worst-case memory and throughput envelopes upfront. When an invariant is breached or backpressure fails, the system surfaces the violation immediately and deterministically at the exact point of overflow. This turns a latent, hard-to-diagnose production outage into an obvious, localized failure that is far easier to detect during testing and contain in production.

models.label: GPT-6.2-Sol
models.answer:
An unbounded collection can hide a slow buildup of state. A missed cleanup, a trickle of stale entries, or a producer that consistently outruns its consumer may cause no obvious trouble for months. Eventually, the accumulated state can increase latency, exhaust memory, or bring down the process far from the code that caused the growth.

A fixed capacity paired with an assertion turns the expected maximum into a checked invariant. If the collection reaches that limit, the system can flag the problem where the growth occurs, making it easier to diagnose before it consumes the process’s memory budget.

Even a small, persistent mismatch between how fast items arrive and how fast they leave can go unnoticed in tests. A fixed capacity makes the expected maximum explicit. With an assertion active, the first insertion that would exceed the limit flags the problem where it occurs, while the cause is easier to diagnose.
